fact_en:
Why do your eyes blink so fast sometimes?

When something suddenly comes near your face, your eye snaps shut instantly as a reflex to protect itself — even before you decide to blink!
fact_bis:
Ngano kusog usahay mopiyong ang mata?

Kon adunay kalit nga moduol sa imong nawong, kusog nga mopiyong ang mata nga paspas kaayo isip reflex aron manalipod, bisan dili nimo tuyo!

findings.note: title_bis "Reflex nga Kislap sa Panalipod" for title_en "Blinking Guards the Eye". Kislap is sparkle/flash -- the corpus uses it for stars, fireflies and electric sparks ("Kislap sa Alitaptap", "Kislap sa Bituon Dili Planeta", "Kislap Karga Lukso Hangin") -- while its word for blinking is kurap ("Kurap Batok sa Abog", "Reflex nga Pagkurap", "Walay Kurap nga Mata sa Insekto"). The title names a flashing/sparkling eye instead of a blink. Weakest of the four: the body restores the action plainly ("kusog nga mopiyong ang mata ... isip reflex aron manalipod"), so this is a title-only scan-level defect.

fact_en: A color blind person may find it hard to read traffic lights or tell if a fruit is ripe just by its color.
fact_bis: Ang tawo nga color blind mahimong maglisod pag-ila sa ilaw sa trapiko o kung hinog na ba ang prutas pinaagi sa kolor niini.

findings.note: title_bis "Color Blind Sugnod Prutas Lisod" for title_en "Color Blind Traffic Fruit". Cebuano sugnod = firewood/fuel, and the corpus uses it that way consistently and correctly ("Ipil-Ipil nga Sugnod", "Init sa Sugnod", "Gasoline isip Sugnod"); the corpus's own word for a traffic light is suga (ffct-26029 / ffct-26275 "Traffic Light" => "Suga sa Trapiko"). The title names firewood where the card is about traffic lights. Same substitution elsewhere: ffct-22943 "Daylight Instead of Lights" => "...Imbes Sugnod", ffct-23515 "Bulb Converts to Light" => "Bombilya Kuryente sa Sugnod", ffct-01526 "Termites Confused by Lights" => "...sa Sugnod". Body is correct ("ilaw sa trapiko"), so the defect is confined to the title.

fact_en: In meiosis, each sex cell gets only half the chromosomes — just one from every pair found in the parent cell.
fact_bis: Sa meiosis, ang matag sex cell makadawat lamang og katunga sa kromosoma — usa lang sa matag paris gikan sa selula sa ginikanan.

findings.note: title_bis "Meiosis sa Kalimot" for title_en "Meiosis Halves Chromosomes". Cebuano kalimot = forgetting (kalimot/nakalimot appears corpus-wide only in that sense, e.g. "Ayaw kalimoti ang payong"); half is katunga, which the card's own body uses correctly ("makadawat lamang og katunga sa kromosoma"). The title a child scans says "Meiosis of forgetting" -- the halving, which is the entire point of the card, is absent from it. Confirmed systematic, not a one-off typo: ffct-?? "Charon, Half of Pluto" => "Charon, Kalimot sa Pluto" makes the same substitution.

fact_en: Birds use the colors of their feathers for two reasons: to hide from enemies by blending in, or to attract a mate with bright, showy colors.
fact_bis: Gamiton sa langgam ang kolor sa balhibo niini sa duha ka paagi: aron motago gikan sa kaaway, o aron makadani og kapikas gamit ang hayag nga kolor.

findings.note: title_bis "Buhok sa Tago ug Show" for title_en "Feathers Hide or Show". Cebuano buhok = the hair on a person's head (corpus uses it correctly that way: "Melanin nga Kolor sa Buhok", "Keratin sa Buhok Kuko"); bird feathers are balhibo/balahibo, which this card's own body uses ("ang kolor sa balhibo niini") and which the corpus uses in the parallel titles ("Balahibo sa Agila", "Mga Klase sa Balhibo"). The title tells a child the card is about birds' head-hair. Systematic: ffct-04661 "Feathers Push Air for Flight" => "Buhok sa Lupad sa Langgam", ffct-04093 "Feathers Cover Bird Bodies" => "Buhok nga Motabon sa Langgam".

fact_en: Yogurt gets its tangy taste and texture from two tiny helpers — Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus — bacteria that work together as a team.
fact_bis: Ang yogurt adunay pait nga lami ug texture tungod sa duha ka klase sa bakterya — ang Lactobacillus bulgaricus ug Streptococcus thermophilus — nga magtinabangay sa paghimo niini.

findings.note: Yogurt's flavour is given as "pait nga lami" = BITTER taste; the English says tangy (aslom/maaslom). Bitter is a distinct, wrong taste and nothing later in the card corrects it, so a child reading only the Cebuano learns yogurt tastes bitter. Lower severity than the others — the bacteria fact itself survives — but the taste claim is a factual property of the card and stands uncorrected.

fact_en:
How many ants can live in one colony?

A single leafcutter ant colony can hold up to eight million worker ants, all living together in underground tunnels covering 30 square meters!
fact_bis:
Pila ka langgam ang mahimong mopuyo sa usa ka kolonya?

Ang usa ka kolonya sa leafcutter ant mahimong adunay hangtod walo ka milyon ka mga trabahante nga langgam, nga nagpuyo sa ilawom sa yuta nga nag-abot og 30 ka square meters!

findings.note: Leafcutter ant card calls the ants `langgam` twice — in Cebuano `langgam` is a BIRD (Tagalog false friend). The question reads "Pila ka langgam ang mahimong mopuyo sa usa ka kolonya?" and the answer "walo ka milyon ka mga trabahante nga langgam" = eight million worker BIRDS living in underground tunnels. The stray English "leafcutter ant" and the title `hantik` do not undo a child reading 8 million birds in one colony. Note: this looks systematic — ~47 cards corpus-wide pair English "ant" with `langgam`, though several correctly use `hantik`, `hulmigas`, or `subay`.

fact_en:
Does the makahiya have thorns?

No — the makahiya has no thorns on its stem! It protects itself by quickly folding its leaves whenever you touch it.
fact_bis:
Naay tunok ba ang makahiya?

Wala diay tunok sa tangkay niini! Gipanalipdan sa makahiya ang kaugalingon pinaagi sa dali nga pag-uyog sa mga dahon kon mahikap nimo kini.

findings.note: Makahiya's one and only fact is its defense mechanism, and the Cebuano states the wrong mechanism: "pinaagi sa dali nga pag-uyog sa mga dahon" = by quickly SHAKING its leaves. The plant folds/closes its leaves (motikom / mokumo / pagpilo); `uyog` means to shake or sway (the corpus itself uses `pag-uyog` for earthquake shaking). Nothing else in the card restores the folding, so a child ends up believing makahiya shakes its leaves when touched.

fact_en: A manta ray has two horn-like fins on its head that guide food straight into its mouth!
fact_bis: Ang manta ray adunay duha ka morag-sungay nga bagolbagol sa ulo nga mogiya sa pagkaon padulong sa iyang baba!

findings.note: Manta ray's head fins are rendered `bagolbagol` = SKULL (the corpus uses `bagolbagol` for skull in 6 other cards: helmet, brain protection, calcium). The emphasised phrase reads "duha ka morag-sungay nga bagolbagol sa ulo" = two horn-like skulls on its head. The correct word `kapay` appears only in the title, never in the sentence itself, so the body asserts a different body part than the English.

fact_en:
Why do bark-colored moths survive more?

Birds can't spot them! Moths whose color matches the tree bark hide better, so more survive and reproduce — that's natural selection at work.
fact_bis:
Ngano nga daghan pang naluwas ang anuplos nga kolor-kahoy?

Kay lisod sila makita sa langgam! Ang anuplos nga kolor mohaom sa panit sa kahoy mao nga mas daghan ang maluwas ug manganak — mao kini ang natural selection.

findings.note: Card is about bark-coloured MOTHS and natural selection. title_bis correctly says 'Anunugba' (moth), but the body twice calls the animal 'anuplos' — the stinging/hairy caterpillar (Tagalog higad), a different creature. Corpus check: 'anuplos' occurs in this one card only, while 'anunugba' is used in 33 other moth cards, so it is an outlier slip rather than regional variation. Medium confidence on flag-worthiness: the science (camouflage -> survival) still lands and the title carries the right word, but the Q&A body names the wrong animal throughout.

fact_en: Nutmeg spice comes from the dried seed inside the nutmeg tree's fruit — prized for its warm, fragrant flavor.
fact_bis: Ang nutmeg usa ka panimpla nga gikan sa uga nga liso sulod sa bunga sa kahoy nga nutmeg — ilado tungod sa humot ug init nga lami niini.

findings.note: title_bis 'Paminta nga Nutmeg' asserts nutmeg is a paminta (black pepper) — a different spice entirely; EN title is just 'Nutmeg Spice'. The body does call it 'usa ka panimpla ... gikan sa uga nga liso', which restores the category, so this is title-only, but it is the same shape as the known cat-titled-iro defect: a child reading the heading learns nutmeg is a kind of pepper. Corpus uses 'panakot/panimpla' for spice and reserves 'paminta' for black pepper (ffct-02639, ffct-06463), so the grep pair is real but will also hit legitimate pepper cards.

fact_en:
Why are coral and jellyfish relatives?

Because a coral polyp's tentacles carry tiny stinging cells — like little harpoons — used to catch and stun tiny floating prey, just like jellyfish do!
fact_bis:
Ngano nga managhigala ang coral ug dikya?

Kay ang galamay sa coral polyp adunay gagmayng manunusok nga selula — sama sa gamayng pana — nga gigamit sa pagdakop ug pagpaalup sa gagmayng tukbonon, sama sa dikya!

findings.note: EN asks why coral and jellyfish are RELATIVES (same cnidarian group). The Bisaya question asks 'Ngano nga managhigala ang coral ug dikya?' — managhigala = they are FRIENDS, not kin. The answer only says corals have stinging cells 'sama sa dikya' (like jellyfish) and never states they belong to the same group, so the relatedness fact the card exists to teach is not recoverable from the Cebuano; a child is left with a nonsense 'corals and jellyfish are friends' claim. Corpus note: 'managhigala' is used for English 'relatives' in exactly 3 cards (ffct-02117 butterfly/moth, ffct-09878 nodes/tonsils) — in ffct-02117 the answer restores it ('sakop sila sa usa ka grupo'), here nothing does.

fact_en: A caterpillar eats a lot, especially leaves, so it can grow quickly before it becomes a pupa.
fact_bis: Mokaon og daghan ang ulod, ilabi na og dahon, aron paspas nga modako sa dili pa mahimong pupa.

findings.note: title_bis is "Hantak" for title_en "Caterpillar". In Cebuano `hantak` is a coin-toss gambling game (and, regionally, a bean) — not a caterpillar, which is `ulod` / `til-as` (the body correctly uses `ulod`). The card label a child sees names a completely different thing. Same defect recurs at ffct-13301 (089.json, title_bis "Yugto sa Hantak"); corpus-wide `hantak` appears only in these two caterpillar titles.
